# Nobody can say what the avatar size limit actually is

## Problem Description

`src/avatar.js` validates the size of an uploaded avatar. The help centre says
"up to 5 MB" and the module works in bytes.

Two tickets landed the same week. One user uploaded a file their operating
system displayed as 5.2 MB and it went through. Another uploaded a file
displayed as exactly 5 MB and got it back rejected. Both users quoted the
help-centre number at us and neither of us could say who was right, because
the tests never go near either limit.

The module also has a floor, meant to catch truncated uploads, and that has
never been exercised either. The single existing test uses a mid-sized file.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/avatar.test.js` giving both size limits systematic edge coverage,
   expressed in the unit the module actually compares in.
2. Include a representative accepted, undersized, and oversized file that is
   nowhere near a limit, so a reader can see the ordinary behaviour of each
   outcome separately from the edges.
3. Every rejecting case asserts the specific code, not merely that the call
   failed.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
5. Do not edit `src/avatar.js`, and leave `src/avatar.smoke.test.js` in place.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/avatar.test.js` giving both size limits systematic edge coverage,
   expressed in the unit the module actually compares in.
2. Include a representative accepted, undersized, and oversized file that is
   nowhere near a limit, so a reader can see the ordinary behaviour of each
   outcome separately from the edges.
3. Every rejecting case asserts the specific code, not merely that the call
   failed.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
5. Do not edit `src/avatar.js`, and leave `src/avatar.smoke.test.js` in place.
assertions: A file src/avatar.test.js exists and contains at least one test that imports validateAvatar.

All three of 1023 (TOO_SMALL), 1024 (accepted), and 1025 (accepted) appear as cases with the correct expectation. Values expressed as arithmetic on MIN_BYTES count. Missing 1025 caps this at half; missing two of the three scores zero.

All three of 5242879 (accepted), 5242880 (accepted), and 5242881 (TOO_LARGE) appear as cases with the correct expectation. Values written as 5 * 1024 * 1024 arithmetic or as MAX_BYTES plus or minus 1 count. Missing 5242879 caps this at half; missing two of the three scores zero.

The values carrying the upper adjacency are one byte apart around 5242880. A suite whose upper cases are 5000000 and 5000001, or 5 MB plus or minus 1 MB, or any pair straddling a decimal-megabyte figure, has left the real adjacency untested and scores zero on this criterion. Extra decimal-unit cases alongside correct byte-resolution ones are harmless, but the byte-resolution ones must be present.

The suite covers at least one accepted size well inside the range (for example 204800), at least one undersized value that is not adjacent to the floor (for example 0 or 100), and at least one oversized value that is not adjacent to the ceiling (for example 10485760). These are separate from the edge cases and none may be within one byte of a limit. Covering only one of the three classes scores zero; covering two caps this at half.

At least one case supplies a value that is not a non-negative safe integer - a fraction, a negative number, a numeric string, null, or a value above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER - and asserts BAD_BYTE_LENGTH.

Failing cases assert the exact code - TOO_SMALL, TOO_LARGE, BAD_BYTE_LENGTH - rather than only that ok is false. Asserting only falsiness scores zero here: a size rejected for the wrong reason would still pass.

Each size is its own test, or is generated per-size by a loop or table-driven helper that yields an individually named case naming the byte count. A single test function holding every assertion scores zero.

# Campaign budget rules are tested at one arbitrary pair of values

## Problem Description

`src/campaign.js` validates the two budget fields on an ad campaign. Both are
whole cents. One of them has fixed limits. The other does not: its floor is
whatever the first field was set to on the same request, so where that floor
sits changes from request to request.

An advertiser on our largest daily cap had a campaign rejected with a message
about the total budget being too low, for a total that would have been fine on
a smaller cap. Nobody could say whether that was correct behaviour, because
the only test we have uses one comfortable pair of numbers and the moving
floor has never been exercised anywhere except at whatever value that test
happens to use.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/campaign.test.js` giving every limit in this module systematic
   edge coverage.
2. The limit that moves must be covered where it actually moves to - not at a
   single convenient setting of the field it depends on.
3. Every rejecting case asserts the specific code, not merely that the request
   was refused.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
5. Do not edit `src/campaign.js`, and leave `src/campaign.smoke.test.js` in
   place.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/campaign.test.js` giving every limit in this module systematic
   edge coverage.
2. The limit that moves must be covered where it actually moves to - not at a
   single convenient setting of the field it depends on.
3. Every rejecting case asserts the specific code, not merely that the request
   was refused.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
5. Do not edit `src/campaign.js`, and leave `src/campaign.smoke.test.js` in
   place.
assertions: A file src/campaign.test.js exists and contains at least one test that imports validateCampaign.

Daily caps 999 (DAILY_CAP_TOO_LOW), 1000 (accepted), 1001 (accepted), 99999 (accepted), 100000 (accepted), and 100001 (DAILY_CAP_TOO_HIGH) each appear with the correct expectation, with the total budget held at a value comfortably inside its own range. Covering one end fully and the other with only the limit itself caps this at half; covering fewer than four of the six points scores zero.

With dailyCapCents at 1000, total budgets 999 (TOTAL_BELOW_DAILY_CAP), 1000 (accepted), and 1001 (accepted) each appear with the correct expectation. Missing 1001 caps this at half; missing two of the three scores zero.

With dailyCapCents at 100000, total budgets 99999 (TOTAL_BELOW_DAILY_CAP), 100000 (accepted), and 100001 (accepted) each appear with the correct expectation. This is the criterion the task exists for: probing the floor at only one daily cap - however thoroughly - scores zero here, because a comparison hard-coded against a constant floor passes every such case. Probing a second daily cap that is not at the top of its range but is clearly different from the first (for example 50000) caps this at half.

Total budgets 9999999 (accepted), 10000000 (accepted), and 10000001 (TOTAL_BUDGET_TOO_HIGH) each appear with the correct expectation, with the daily cap held inside its range. Missing 9999999 caps this at half; missing two of the three scores zero.

Each pair of values is its own test case, or is generated per-pair by a loop or table-driven helper that yields an individually named case naming both amounts. A single test function asserting every pair in sequence scores zero: the first failing pair hides every later one, and with a floor that moves between cases that is exactly the information needed to localise the bug.

Failing cases assert the exact code - DAILY_CAP_TOO_LOW, DAILY_CAP_TOO_HIGH, TOTAL_BELOW_DAILY_CAP, TOTAL_BUDGET_TOO_HIGH, and the integer-check codes - rather than only that ok is false. Asserting only falsiness scores zero here: a total budget of 999 against a daily cap of 1000 and a daily cap of 999 are different failures that a falsiness-only suite cannot separate.

Every probed pair is written as literals or derived arithmetically from the exported MIN_DAILY_CAP / MAX_DAILY_CAP / MAX_TOTAL_BUDGET. Pairs drawn from Math.random or an unseeded generator score zero here, since the floor under test then differs run to run.

   behaviour was determined from the implementation and not from the wording.
3. Every rejecting case asserts the specific code, not merely that the order
   was ineligible.

Item counts 99 (eligible), 100 (eligible), and 101 (TOO_MANY_ITEMS) each appear with the correct expectation. The case on 100 must exist and assert that the order still qualifies - that is one of the two questions support asked. Missing 99 caps this at half; missing the case on 100 scores zero.

# Display-name limits have never been tested with anything but plain letters

## Problem Description

`src/display-name.js` enforces two separate limits on a profile display name:
a product limit on how many characters a name may contain, and a storage
limit imposed by the column the name is written to. The two limits count in
different units, and the file says which is which.

The bug that started this: a user in Japan set a name of well under twenty
characters and got a rejection our support team could not explain, because the
name was obviously short. A second user set a name that looked like five
characters to everyone who saw the screenshot and was told it was too long.

Every test we have uses lowercase ASCII, which is exactly the input for which
the two units cannot be told apart, so the suite has never once distinguished
them.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/display-name.test.js` giving both limits systematic edge coverage.
2. The storage limit must actually be reached by at least one case - work out
   what kind of input can reach it without tripping the character limit first.
3. Include at least one name whose visible character count, as a person would
   count it on screen, differs from the count this module uses, and record in
   a test name or comment which count the module applies.
4. Every rejecting case asserts the specific code, not merely that the name
   was refused.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
6. Do not edit `src/display-name.js`, and leave `src/display-name.smoke.test.js`
   in place.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/display-name.test.js` giving both limits systematic edge coverage.
2. The storage limit must actually be reached by at least one case - work out
   what kind of input can reach it without tripping the character limit first.
3. Include at least one name whose visible character count, as a person would
   count it on screen, differs from the count this module uses, and record in
   a test name or comment which count the module applies.
4. Every rejecting case asserts the specific code, not merely that the name
   was refused.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
6. Do not edit `src/display-name.js`, and leave `src/display-name.smoke.test.js`
   in place.
assertions: A file src/display-name.test.js exists and contains at least one test that imports validateDisplayName.

Names of 0 characters (empty string, TOO_SHORT), 1 character (accepted), and 2 characters (accepted) each appear with the correct expectation. Missing the 2-character case caps this at half; missing two of the three scores zero.

Names of 23 (accepted), 24 (accepted), and 25 (TOO_LONG) code points each appear with the correct expectation - for example 'a'.repeat(23) / .repeat(24) / .repeat(25). Missing the 23-code-point case caps this at half; missing two of the three scores zero.

At least one case asserts the STORAGE_OVERFLOW code, and the limit is probed on all three points using astral characters so the character limit does not fire first: '\u{1F600}'.repeat(19) = 19 code points / 38 units (accepted), .repeat(20) = 20 code points / 40 units (accepted), .repeat(21) = 21 code points / 42 units (STORAGE_OVERFLOW). Any astral character works in place of U+1F600. No case producing STORAGE_OVERFLOW anywhere scores zero on this criterion - that branch is unreachable with ASCII input, and leaving it uncovered is the whole gap. Producing STORAGE_OVERFLOW but with no accepted case at exactly 40 units caps this at half.

At least one accepted or TOO_LONG case uses a string whose UTF-16 length differs from its code-point count while sitting on the character limit - for example '\u{1F600}'.repeat(8) + 'a'.repeat(16) is 24 code points in 32 units (accepted) and '\u{1F600}'.repeat(8) + 'a'.repeat(17) is 25 code points in 33 units (TOO_LONG). A suite in which every character-limit probe is pure ASCII scores zero here: for ASCII the two counts are equal, so the case cannot distinguish a code-point rule from a UTF-16 rule and would still pass if the module counted the wrong one.

At least one case uses a name whose on-screen character count differs from its code-point count - for example '\u{1F469}\u{200D}\u{1F469}\u{200D}\u{1F467}'.repeat(5), which reads as 5 items on screen but is 25 code points and therefore TOO_LONG - and a test name or comment states that the module counts code points, not what a person sees. Having the case but no written note caps this at half; having neither scores zero.

Every probe string is a fixed literal, an escape sequence, or a deterministic repeat. Strings assembled from Math.random, an unseeded generator, or a random pick out of a character pool score zero here: the code-point and UTF-16 counts of the result then differ run to run, so the case can drift off the limit it was written to sit on.

Failing cases assert the exact code - TOO_SHORT, TOO_LONG, STORAGE_OVERFLOW, NOT_A_STRING - rather than only that ok is false, and each probe is its own test or a per-case entry produced by a loop or table-driven helper. Asserting only falsiness scores zero, since TOO_LONG and STORAGE_OVERFLOW are exactly the two outcomes this task is about telling apart. A single test function holding every assertion also scores zero.
